finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the user-supplied token with PHP loose equality (==). If the stored token is a numeric-looking string (e.g. 0e followed by digits, which hex-digest tokens produce occasionally), any other 0e<digits> string such as '0e0' matches. Where the token arrives as a typed value (JSON int/bool/null), type juggling also applies: on PHP 7, 0 == 'abc' is true; on any version, a NULL or empty stored token matches null, '' or false. The attacker can then reset the password for any email they name. The comparison is also not constant-time.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled $email and $token arguments (presumably from the request) to reset_password_loose. The attacker needs a pending reset row for the victim email, which they can trigger via the forgot-password flow.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (line 5): account password takeover.

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for the attacker-chosen email.
$row['token'] == $token is a loose comparison that allows magic-hash and juggling matches. A NULL or empty stored token matches an empty or null attacker token.
The password is overwritten for the victim email.

finding.guards_checked: No strict (===) comparison, hash_equals, or type check on $token in this function. No empty-token check, rate limiting, or expiry. The sibling reset_password() uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, which fixes this. SQL is built with $db->quote(), so no SQL injection. Whether the vulnerable variant is actually called could not be confirmed, because this is the only file.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset_password_loose. Only the SQL-injection guard, $db->quote(), at reset.php:3 and 5-6. The safe sibling reset_password() (reset.php:14) uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but it is a separate function.
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 compares with `==` and has no empty-token, type, expiry or rate-limit check, so a NULL or empty stored token or a numeric-looking "0e…" token can match an attacker-supplied value and reach the password UPDATE at reset.php:5-6; caveat: reset.php is the only file, so I could not see whether callers use this variant or pass attacker-controlled arguments, and a "0e…" match is rare in practice.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (the sibling reset_password() at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with a string cast, but reset_password_loose has no strict comparison, empty-token check, or expiry)
verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:4 uses `$row['token'] == $token` with attacker-supplied $email and $token and no other guard, so loose-comparison matches (a numeric-looking "0e…" stored token, or an empty/NULL stored token) let an anonymous caller reach the password UPDATE at reset.php:5. Exploitability depends on the stored token's shape and the input type, and I could not check which variant callers use.

finding.claim: Neither function invalidates the reset token after a successful reset, and neither checks token expiry or a single-use flag. A leaked, intercepted or old token stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed to reset the password again. Separately, in reset_password() a NULL token column makes hash_equals() throw a TypeError, which is a robustness issue rather than a bypass.
finding.source: Attacker holds a previously issued or leaked reset token (from email, logs or a referer header) for a victim email.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (lines 15-16): repeated or late account takeover.

trace.note: Token row is fetched with no expiry or created_at check.
The token is verified but never consumed.
The password is updated and the function returns true without deleting the resets row, so the same token still works.

finding.guards_checked: No DELETE on the resets table, no expiry column, and no attempt counter appears in the file. Cleanup may happen elsewhere, but no other code exists in this directory.

verdict.reason: reset.php:13-17 selects only `token` with no expiry or created_at check, verifies it with hash_equals, then runs the UPDATE at lines 15-16 and returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row, so a leaked token can be replayed. The directory holds only this file, so any cleanup elsewhere can't be checked.

verdict_facts.reason: reset.php:13-17 selects the token with no expiry check, runs the UPDATE at 15-16 and returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row, and no other file in the directory does so, so a leaked token can be replayed.
